⁣
Martin Scorsese’s The Aviator (2004) is an epic portrait of Howard Hughes, a man who seemed larger than life but was ultimately undone by his own obsessions. It’s not a gangster film, yet it carries all the hallmarks of Scorsese’s style: grand spectacle, flawed characters, and the sense that we are watching life unfold before our eyes.⁣
⁣
Leonardo DiCaprio disappears into Hughes, delivering what many consider his first truly transformative performance. Gone is the “pretty boy” of Titanic (1997). He fully embodies Hughes’s ambition, brilliance, and eventual unraveling. Watching him shift from the confident, movie-making playboy and aviation pioneer to the paranoid loner is harrowing. ⁣
⁣
The film is filled with spectacle: Hughes crashing planes, pushing aviation technology to its limits, and waging war against Pan Am’s monopoly. But the real war is internal: his unstoppable will and the inner demons that haunt him. He builds faster planes, dates Hollywood starlets, and conquers industries, but none of it frees him from the obsessive-compulsive disorder that consumes him. Scorsese and screenwriter John Logan capture Hughes’s contradictions beautifully. He was both visionary and destructive, heroic and pathetic, a man who flew higher than anyone else and crashed harder too. The film never simplifies him, and that complexity is what makes it so good.⁣
⁣
At nearly three hours, the film never felt dull to me. Scorsese has made many masterpieces, but The Aviator (2004) stands tall among them all. Not just as spectacle, but as one of the most moving character studies of his career.

source_details.synopsis: The Aviator is a 2004 epic biographical drama film directed by Martin Scorsese and written by John Logan. It stars Leonardo DiCaprio as Howard Hughes, Cate Blanchett as Katharine Hepburn, and Kate Beckinsale as Ava Gardner. The supporting cast includes John C. Reilly, Alec Baldwin, Alan Alda and Jude Law. The film depicts the life of Howard Hughes, an aviation pioneer and director of the film Hell's Angels (1930). The film portrays his life from 1927 to 1947, when Hughes became a successful film producer and an aviation magnate while simultaneously growing more unstable due to severe obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD).
